documents.title: The unglamorous science of keeping bridges standing
documents.text:
Public attention turns to bridges mainly when one collapses, which obscures the fact that most failures are slow and visible long before they become dangerous. Engineers who inspect the nation's bridges describe a discipline that has more in common with medicine than with construction: a matter of noticing small symptoms and acting on them before they spread.

The commonest culprit is not a design flaw but water. Rain finds its way through cracked joints and into the steel reinforcement, where it causes corrosion that expands and cracks the concrete around it, admitting still more water. The process can take decades, yet it accelerates once begun, which is why inspectors place such emphasis on drainage and sealing, tasks that attract little notice and less funding.

That lack of funding is the central difficulty. A study of one regional authority found that repair costs for a bridge rise roughly fourfold if maintenance is deferred by ten years, yet budgets are typically set annually, and new construction is easier to celebrate than maintenance. "No one cuts a ribbon on a drain," said one inspector.

Some authorities have begun to install sensors that measure moisture and movement continuously. The data, they hope, will allow repairs to be scheduled when they are cheapest, though the sensors themselves must be maintained.

choices: Most bridges fail suddenly without warning

Bridge safety needs dull, neglected upkeep
Sensors have made inspections obsolete
questions.explanation: The article stresses slow water damage and underfunded maintenance.

questions.prompt: According to the article, what causes the commonest damage?
choices: Water entering joints and corroding steel

Mistakes in the original design plans

questions.explanation: Water enters cracked joints and corrodes the reinforcement.

questions.prompt: What does 'No one cuts a ribbon on a drain' suggest?
choices: Drains are very expensive to construct

questions.explanation: New construction is easier to celebrate than maintenance.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the sensors?
choices: They remove the need for yearly budgets
They may time repairs but need care too
They have already prevented a collapse
They are too costly for any authority
questions.explanation: The data may allow cheaper scheduling, though the sensors must be maintained.

documents.title: Request to reconsider a rejected conference proposal
documents.text:
To: Programme Committee, International Congress on Water Policy
From: Dr. Nikolai Petrenko
Subject: Request for reconsideration of submission 214

Dear Committee members,

Thank you for your email of 12 June informing me that my proposed paper, "Pricing and the poor: lessons from three cities", has not been accepted. I understand that the competition was strong, and I do not write to dispute your right to choose. I do, however, wish to ask you to reconsider on one specific ground.

The reviewer's report, which you kindly forwarded, states that the paper "offers no original data". This is not accurate. The paper draws on a household survey of eleven hundred families, which my team conducted last year and which has not previously been published; it is described in the third section of the abstract, and I suspect that the reviewer overlooked it because it follows a long summary of earlier studies.

I have therefore revised the abstract so that the survey appears in the first paragraph, and I enclose the new version. I would not ask you to accept the paper automatically, but I would be grateful if a second reviewer could read the amended text. If this is not possible before the program is finalized, I would be glad to be placed on a waiting list.

With respect and thanks,
Nikolai Petrenko

questions.explanation: The survey now appears in the first paragraph.

documents.title: Notice to library members: changes to borrowing from 1 September
documents.text:
WESTBURY PUBLIC LIBRARY — NOTICE TO MEMBERS

From 1 September, three changes will apply to borrowing at all branches.

First, the limit on items that may be borrowed at one time will rise from ten to fifteen. This change follows a request from many members, particularly families, who found the previous limit restrictive. The limit on audio-visual items, however, will stay at three.

Second, overdue fines will be abolished for all children's books and reduced from 20 cents to 10 cents a day for adult titles, with a maximum of 3 dollars per item. The library council made this decision after finding that fines raised little money and discouraged some families from using the library at all. Items more than thirty days overdue will still be treated as lost, and the replacement cost will be charged.

Third, books may no longer be renewed by telephone. Renewals can be made on the library website, at the self-service machines or in person. Members who have difficulty with these methods may ask a member of staff for help at any branch, and the telephone service will remain available for reservations.

We hope these changes make the library easier to use. Comments are welcome at the main desk.

To announce the closing of a branch
To invite donations of new books
To announce new borrowing and fine rules
questions.explanation: The notice describes three changes effective 1 September.

documents.title: Customer Insights Analyst, Pelham & Rowe Retail
documents.text:
Pelham & Rowe, a regional retailer with ninety stores, is looking for a Customer Insights Analyst to help us understand how and why our customers shop. The role sits within the marketing department and reports to the Head of Analytics.

You will work with sales data, loyalty-card records and survey results to identify patterns in customer behavior, and you will present your findings to colleagues who are not specialists. Your work will inform decisions on which products we stock, how we price them and where we open new stores. A recent project, for example, showed that shoppers who bought a particular brand of coffee were far more likely to buy a premium cheese, a discovery that led to a change in the layout of forty stores.

The ideal candidate has at least three years' experience of analysis, a good command of statistical software and the ability to explain a complex result simply. Experience in retail is helpful but not essential; we are more interested in curiosity and clarity than in knowledge of our sector. Because the role involves frequent presentations, confidence in speaking to groups is important.

We offer a hybrid working pattern, with two days a week in our Leeds office. Applications should include a sample of previous work, with any confidential figures removed, and should reach us by 15 July.

questions.prompt: What is the main responsibility of the post?
choices: Turning shopper data into advice
Managing the daily sales in each store
Designing new loyalty cards for shoppers
Selling products directly to customers
questions.explanation: The analyst studies data and presents findings to inform decisions.

questions.prompt: What example shows the value of the work?
choices: A new store was opened in the city of Leeds
A price cut doubled sales of the coffee
A coffee and cheese link changed layouts
A survey led to forty stores closing
questions.explanation: The coffee-cheese pattern led to a layout change in forty stores.

questions.prompt: What does the ad imply about the retail experience requirement?
choices: Only retail veterans are ever considered
The firm will train good candidates in retail
The company prefers analysts with no curiosity
Retail knowledge matters more than clarity
questions.explanation: Experience in retail is helpful but not essential; curiosity and clarity matter more.

questions.prompt: What must applicants include?
choices: A letter from a store manager in the chain
A list of their favorite retail brands
A certificate in marketing or analytics
A sample of past work, figures removed
questions.explanation: A sample of previous work with confidential figures removed.

documents.title: Messages between a landlord and a tenant
documents.text:
Landlord (Mr. Farrow) [9:10]: Good morning, Ms. Ito. I'm writing about the boiler. The engineer can come on Thursday between 8 and 12 to replace the valve, but someone must be there to let him in.

Tenant (Ms. Ito) [9:14]: I work on Thursdays, I'm afraid. Could he come on Friday instead?

Mr. Farrow [9:16]: Friday is difficult. He's booked on another job all day, and the next free slot is the following Tuesday.

Ms. Ito [9:18]: That's a long wait, since the heating has been off since Sunday. Could my neighbor let him in? She has a spare key to my flat.

Mr. Farrow [9:21]: Normally I'd prefer that I or my agent be present, but in the circumstances that seems reasonable, provided she agrees and you confirm in writing that she may enter.

Ms. Ito [9:23]: I'll ask her this afternoon and send you an email tonight.

Mr. Farrow [9:24]: Thank you. I'll tell the engineer to expect her. I should also mention that if the valve doesn't fix the fault, he may need to order a part, which would take about a week.

Ms. Ito [9:26]: Understood. Let's hope it doesn't come to that.

documents.title: What happens to a language when its last teacher retires
documents.text:
In the highland villages of the northern province, the language of the Taru people is spoken daily by only a few hundred elderly residents. Younger people understand it but answer in the national language, and the single remaining school that teaches it is due to close next year, when its only qualified teacher, Mrs. Anwen Tilu, reaches retirement age.

Linguists often describe such moments as the point of no return, since a language that is not learned at school has little chance of being passed on at home. Yet local efforts suggest that the story may not be settled. A group of young parents has begun to hold weekly evenings at which elders tell stories and children repeat them, and a recording project funded by a university has produced nearly two hundred hours of speech.

Specialists, however, are cautious. Recordings preserve a language but do not keep it alive, and an evening club cannot replace daily use. "The risk is that people feel they have done something, and stop," said one researcher.

Mrs. Tilu is not despondent. She has begun to train two former pupils as teachers, though the provincial government has not yet promised to pay them. "A language lives where there is someone who needs it," she says, "and I believe my pupils will find such a place."

choices: A school has just been opened for the language

questions.explanation: It describes the decline and the local attempts to revive the language.

choices: The recordings are of poor quality

questions.explanation: Recordings preserve but do not keep a language alive; people 'feel they have done something, and stop'.

choices: Language is a matter of school grades

questions.explanation: A language lives where there is someone who needs it.

documents.title: Letter of apology from a travel company
documents.text:
Dear Mr. and Mrs. Valdivia,

Thank you for your letter of 30 September about your recent holiday to the Algarve. I have read it twice, and I wish to apologize without reservation for the experience you describe.

You were promised a sea-view room and were placed in one overlooking the car park for the first four nights. The hotel has explained that a group booking caused an overflow, but that does not excuse the fact that we did not warn you. You also report that the airport transfer was ninety minutes late, a delay that my colleagues attribute to a driver's illness, though I recognize that this is little consolation after a night flight.

We cannot return the time that you lost, but we can offer some redress. I enclose a refund of 480 dollars, which represents the difference in price between the room you booked and the one you received, together with a voucher for 250 dollars towards a future holiday. I hope you will accept it in the spirit in which it is offered, as an acknowledgement of failure and not as an attempt to buy your silence.

We have also asked the hotel for a written explanation, which I shall forward when it arrives.

Yours sincerely,
Rowena Ashby, Customer Relations
